(1) the percent tumor necro-sis after chemotherapy is an impor-tant prognostic indicator; and (2) areas of tumor carti-lage or widely distributed, mi-totically-inactive atypical cells should be excluded from the calculation of the percent tumor nec-rosis.

(1) areas of tumor cartilge or isolated atypical cells do not represent viable osteosarcoma; (2) the percentage of viable osteosarcomatous tissue is an important prognositic indicator of disease-free survival; and (3) the percentage of necrosis is an important prognositic indicator of disease-free survial.
the presence of tumor cartilage and widely dispersed, isolated, atypical cells in osteosarcoma does not predict an adverse outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a new method for the quantitative assessment of tumor response in osteosarcoma.
the development of a new method of treatment of osteosarcoma.
the development of a new method for measuring tumor necrosis in osteosarcoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the “stringent method” is the best method for assessing the amount of tumor necrosis after neoadjuvant therapy for osteosarcoma.

the presence of residual tumor cartilage and/or widely distributed, atypical, non-mitotic cells is not prognostically significant and should not be included in the calculation of percent tumor necrosis in osteosarcoma.
the presence of residual tumor in osteosarcoma is prognostically significant, but the pattern of viable tumor (e.g. tumor cartilage, widely scattered atypical cells in stroma or fibrosis) is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of tumor cartilage and/or isolated atypical cells is not prognostic of outcome in osteosarcoma.
residual tumor cartilage and isolated atypical cells are not prognostically significant and should be ignored.
the “stringent method” of evaluating tumor necrosis is a more reliable prognostic indicator for disease-free survival than the “inclusive method”.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of residual tumor cartilage in osteosarcomatous tissue after chemotherapy is not associated with poor outcome.
the presence of residual tumor in a patient with osteosarcoma does not always indicate that the patient will not survive.
the presence of tumor cartilage and/or isolated atypical cells should be excluded from the calculation of tumor necrosis after neoadjuvant treatment of osteosarcoma.
